title: 02 - Theories of the State

content.text: Syllabus — Theories of the State: Liberal, Neo-liberal, Marxist, Pluralist, Post-colonial and Feminist. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 2)

the concept & elements of the state; theories of sovereignty (monistic/Austin vs pluralist) and the impact of globalization on sovereignty; and the six theories of the state — Liberal (negative, positive, neo-liberal), Marxist (instrumentalist & structuralist), Pluralist, Post-colonial and Feminist — plus the Fascist, Gandhian and legitimacy-crisis conceptions and the crisis of the modern nation-state.

Hobbes, Locke, Austin, Laski, MacIver, Krabbe, Marx, Engels, Lenin, Miliband, Poulantzas, Gramsci, Robert Dahl, C. Wright Mills, Kenichi Ohmae, David Held, Edward Said, Hamza Alavi, A.G. Frank, Wallerstein, Gunnar Myrdal, F.W. Riggs, Catherine MacKinnon, Carole Pateman, Mussolini, Gandhi, Habermas.

the heaviest-scoring unit. Neo-liberal state (2016/17/18), Feminist (2021), Post-colonial (2020), Pluralist (2019), Marxist & materialism (2013/14), sovereignty & globalization (2015), Gandhi (2015), Fascism (2014/18), legitimacy crisis (2015), Hobbesian obligation (2017).

Q — Trace the evolution of the liberal theory of the state through its negative, positive and neo-liberal phases, and critically examine the neo-liberal conception of the state and its link with globalization. (UPSC 2016/2017/2018)
Tell the story of liberalism in three phases → then judge neo-liberalism and its marriage with globalization.
— a neutral, limited state resting on consent;
(The state is the referee, not a player — it enforces the rules of the market but never picks the winner.)
— the state keeps law and order and enforces contracts — nothing more.
— the simple absence of interference, so the less the state does the freer the citizen.
— the state creates the conditions of self-development.
— free speech is empty for a hungry illiterate — hence MGNREGA and the Right to Education.
roll the welfare ‘nanny state’ back on three counts:
— India’s 1991 LPG reforms: the licence raj dismantled, PSUs disinvested.
: economic freedom is a precondition of political freedom.
— neo-liberalism became globalization’s ideology through three carriers:
— the doctrine adopted by the leading states and exported as ‘shock therapy’.
— IMF loans carried structural-adjustment conditions, as with India in 1991.
(The 2008 bailouts brought the state straight back.)
The liberal theory sees the state as a
that exists to protect individual rights and freedom and rests on the
. It is a referee rather than a player: it lays down and enforces the rules within which individuals pursue their own ends, but does not prescribe those ends.

caught the ambivalence in calling it a ‘necessary evil’ — evil because every law restricts freedom, necessary because freedom cannot be safeguarded without it. From this single premise the doctrine evolved through three phases.
Adam Smith, Bentham, James Mill, Herbert Spencer
) begins from the rational individual possessing inalienable rights to life, liberty and property. From that premise it builds two pillars:
— the state must confine itself to defence, law and order and the enforcement of contracts, since the market coordinates society better than any minister can.
— liberty is the mere absence of external interference, so that the less the state does, the freer the citizen is held to be.
By the late nineteenth century laissez-faire had produced liberty without equality, and welfare liberals (
) recast the state in two connected moves:
— the state becomes responsible for the conditions of self-development, which require education, health and a floor of income.

— liberty is not being left alone but possessing the actual capacity for self-development. Freedom of speech means little to a hungry illiterate; hence the welfare state, and in India measures such as MGNREGA and the Right to Education, are read as enabling rather than restricting freedom.
) is a reaction against this interventionist ‘nanny state’, which it charges with inefficiency, dependence and creeping serfdom. Its programme has three elements:
— the state is rolled back to its minimal functions; India’s 1991 liberalisation, dismantling the licence raj and disinvesting public undertakings, is the clearest domestic instance.
— “economic freedom is a precondition of political freedom” (
declares that “social justice is a mirage” because market outcomes are unintended and so cannot be called unjust.
Neo-liberalism became the ruling ideology of globalization, carried by three vehicles:
, it was exported through ‘shock therapy’ and structural adjustment.

was its institutional high point, and loans carried conditionalities obliging borrowing states to shrink themselves, as India experienced in 1991; hence the examiner’s proposition that “the political ideology of globalization is neo-liberalism.”
By overestimating the individual and underestimating the state, liberalism builds a capitalist order that can serve exploitative ends, and neo-liberalism’s widening inequality has produced a
, for whom development is the expansion of capabilities, and
, who exposes the asymmetries of globalization, therefore argue for a balanced, welfare-oriented state — a case vindicated by the post-2008 return of massive state intervention.
Q — Examine the Marxist theory of the state — its origin, its instrumentalist and relative-autonomy (structuralist) variants, and its materialist basis. (UPSC 2013/2014)
Show why the state is a class weapon → prove the materialist basis → contrast the two Marxist variants → end with withering away.
— the state is not neutral but a
(The colonial state’s law protected the planter, never the tenant.)
— politics rests on economics, in two tiers:
— the mode of production and whoever owns the means of production.
— law, politics and ideas, the state among them.
(Whoever owns the factory shapes who writes the factory law.)
: the state is the ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’.
(Even the welfare state left wealth concentrated and the bureaucracy elitist.)
— it may act against individual capitalists to save capitalism itself, legislating a minimum wage in calm times.
— but it bails out the banks in a crash — 2008.
: rule works by consent, not coercion alone.
(Schools and the press make the ruler’s worldview feel like common sense.)
— the state lasts only as long as classes do.
: not all conflict is class conflict; yet no theory exposes the state’s hidden class bias better.
Marxism is above all a critique of the liberal-capitalist state. Against the liberal claim of neutrality it argues that the state is a
— an instrument of organised coercion serving whichever class owns the means of production. Its origin lies not in a social contract but in
and in the splitting of society into contending classes: for
The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State
, the state arises precisely when class antagonism becomes unmanageable — as the colonial state’s codes protected the planter and never the tenant.
Marx’s understanding is materialistic because politics is determined by economics, society being read in two tiers:
— the mode of production and the class owning it; whoever owns the factory ultimately shapes who writes the factory law.

— law, politics, religion and ideas, the state among them, all determined by the base. Political power is thus ‘the organised power of one class for oppressing another’, and ‘the ruling ideas of every age are the ideas of the ruling class’: the state cannot float free of the property relations that sustain it.
) the state is a direct tool in the hands of the capitalists — “the executive committee of the bourgeoisie” (
), which “represents the irreconcilability of class antagonism” (

, showed empirically that even in the post-war welfare state wealth remained concentrated and the higher bureaucracy, judiciary and army were recruited from the propertied elite — exploding the myth of a ‘managerial revolution’.

— it is not a puppet, and where no single class is dominant it can act as an ‘equilibrium-maker’ above classes, as under Bonapartism, thereby appearing neutral. It may even legislate against particular capitalists — a minimum wage, a factory safety law — in order to preserve capitalism as a whole.
— in a genuine crisis it intervenes for the rich, as the 2008 bank bailouts amid ‘Occupy Wall Street’ revealed.
Two further propositions complete the theory:

showed that class rule survives less through force than through the manufacture of consent in civil society, so that schools, churches and newspapers make the ruling class’s worldview feel like plain common sense.

— the state is nevertheless historical, not eternal: it exists only as long as classes exist, and once the dictatorship of the proletariat has abolished private property it will ‘wither away’ in a classless communist society.

and the pluralists object that the theory reduces all conflict to class conflict, ignoring the real competition of religious, linguistic, regional and professional groups, while twentieth-century experience suggests the state does not wither but hardens. Yet the Marxist theory remains the sharpest available exposure of the class bias concealed behind the state’s claim to neutrality.
Q — Critically examine the pluralist theory of the state and sovereignty as an attack on the monistic (Austinian) theory. (UPSC 2019)
State the monistic doctrine → mount the pluralist attack → grade the pluralists → weigh the charge of inconsistency.
sovereign; ‘law is the command of the sovereign’.
(Sovereignty = the last word that no one may lawfully answer back.)
(A citizen’s life is ruled as much by her union, caste panchayat, temple and university.)
— “since society is federal, authority should also be federal”;
: sovereignty must be ‘expunged from political theory’.
(India’s Seventh Schedule and the 73rd Amendment are federal authority in practice.)
: the state is still ‘the keystone of the social architecture’.
— it attacks the state yet keeps it — ‘cake and eat it too’.
5.3 No state ever fitted the model
: not even Ranjit Singh’s Punjab matched Austin.
— inconsistency is not irrelevance: dispersed power fits an age of federalism, the UN and the EU better than war-prone monism.
holds that in every independent political society there must exist one determinate sovereign whose power is
absolute, universal, permanent, indivisible and inalienable

put it formally: if a determinate human superior, not habitually obeying any other superior, receives habitual obedience from the bulk of a given society, that superior is sovereign and ‘law is the command of the sovereign’. Sovereignty is thus the last word to which no one may lawfully answer back — a position echoed in
definition of the state by its monopoly of legitimate force, and rooted in
) deny that any single centre can absorb all authority. Human beings pursue many interests through many associations, so power should be

, not their master, and cannot satisfy the whole of human need. A citizen’s conduct in India is in fact governed as much by her trade union, caste panchayat, religious body and university as by Parliament, and each of these commands a genuine loyalty of its own.

compressed the argument into a maxim: “since society is federal, authority should also be federal.” Sovereignty must be functionally divided among the groups that actually perform society’s work, and obedience must be earned rather than commanded.

went further, insisting that “the notion of sovereignty must be expunged from political theory” and replaced by the sovereignty of law and the community’s sense of right. The Indian Constitution’s distribution of powers in the Seventh Schedule and the devolution effected by the 73rd Amendment illustrate such federal authority in practice.
still makes the state ‘the keystone of the social architecture’, because it alone can resolve conflicts between associations and command the widest allegiance.
allows it no primacy at all: the ‘service state’ “commands because it serves” and is ‘both the guardian and the child of law’, so its authority is derivative and conditional.
Three charges are pressed against the theory:
— it attacks the state’s supremacy yet, unlike anarchism, retains the state, so critics say ‘pluralists want to keep the cake and eat it too’.
— it assumes associations compete on equal terms, whereas
shows a ‘power elite’ of corporate, military and political leaders dominating the rest, a survival of the fittest among groups.
adds that no historical state, Ranjit Singh’s Punjab included, ever matched Austin’s model either.

Inconsistency, however, is not irrelevance. By dispersing power, dignifying associations and taking international law seriously, pluralism describes an age of federalism, the United Nations, the ICJ and the European Union far better than the monistic doctrine, and by denying any state an absolute will it is also the more conducive to peace.
Q — Discuss the theories of sovereignty and examine the challenges posed by globalization to the sovereignty of the modern nation-state. (UPSC 2015)
Define sovereignty and its rival theories → then test how far globalization and internal strains have hollowed it out.
(Only Parliament can bind every person within India’s territory.)
— data and ideas cross frontiers freely.
— a WTO ruling can unsettle a national farm subsidy.
— NGOs and movements press from below.
— no consensus on how far this goes:
— the strain also comes from within:
— the Kurds deny the congruence of nation and state.
— the collapse of the USSR and Yugoslavia.
— no state can any longer guarantee security.
(The EU pools it; climate and trade treaties make India accept limits it writes itself.)

Sovereignty — the supreme and final power to make and enforce law within a territory — is the defining attribute of the modern nation-state and, with population, territory and government, one of its four elements.
supplied its first complete theory in

, where subjects surrender their right of self-government to a single undivided sovereign in exchange for security. In practical terms it means that only Parliament may bind every person within India’s territory, and that externally no other state may command it.
absolute, universal, permanent, indivisible and inalienable
, but two rival accounts divide the field:
, for whom law is simply the command of the sovereign backed by sanction.
insist that authority is shared with the many associations of a federal society, while
would abolish the concept altogether. The globalization debate is in effect the empirical continuation of this old theoretical quarrel.
If the nation-state is a ‘billiard ball with a hard shell’, globalization has made that shell
, concludes that political boundaries are fading as ‘global citizens’ and transnational firms escape state control. The shell is breached on four fronts:
— it carries data and ideas past frontiers.
— it lets capital exit at a keystroke, disciplining national economic policy.
— they bind states from above, so that a WTO ruling can unsettle a national farm subsidy.
— NGOs and movements press from below.
There is no consensus on how far this goes:
hold that sovereignty is genuinely diluted both internally and externally.
reply that the world remains state-centric and that globalization is itself a policy states chose and can reverse.
mediates: globalization is ‘not a zero-sum game’ — in some domains the state loses, in others it gains new regulatory reach — while
notes that weak and strong states are affected very unequally.
The nation-state is strained from within as well, on three counts:
deny the congruence of nation and state.
— federations have disintegrated, as in the USSR and Yugoslavia, while sub-nationalism and diaspora loyalties divide allegiance.
— nuclear weapons mean no state can any longer guarantee the security that was sovereignty’s original justification — producing a ‘global village’ of shared risks, from pandemics to climate change.
Sovereignty is therefore not extinguished but

: because global problems demand collective solutions, states now accept self-imposed adjustments to their own authority, as the European Union’s pooling of sovereignty and India’s climate and trade commitments show.
rightly urges that economics and politics be studied together to grasp this shift of authority from states to markets.
Q — Analyse the post-colonial theory of the state through the modernization and Marxist (dependency/structuralist) perspectives. (UPSC 2020)
Say what makes the post-colonial state distinctive → then read it twice over, once through modernization and once through Marxism.
— newly independent ‘third world’ states still shaped by colonialism;
(Flag independence, while the economy still ships raw material to the old metropolis.)
— two jobs the West never faced at once:
— forging one shared identity across language, caste and religion.
— creating effective authority; India integrated 500-odd princely states.
— two diagnoses of the gap between law and practice:
: formalism, the law on paper differs from the law in the village.
: land-ceiling laws passed everywhere, enforced almost nowhere.
— a rich core and a dependent periphery in unequal exchange — the ‘development of underdevelopment’.
— escape lies in withdrawing from the world market.
— a bureaucracy and army towering over a traditional base.
(Pakistan as a military-bureaucratic oligarchy; India’s ‘inspector raj’.)
— it mediates between metropolitan bourgeoisie, native bourgeoisie and landed classes rather than serving one.
— caught between an imported form and inherited economic dependence, its nation- and state-building remain unfinished.
Post-colonial theory is not a fresh general theory of the state but an attempt to analyse the
whose politics remains shaped by their colonial past. Formal independence coexists with continuing economic and cultural domination — a
, in which a country flies its own flag while still exporting raw material to its former metropolis.
stress how deeply this legacy penetrates knowledge and identity themselves.
the Western state never faced simultaneously, attempting in decades what Europe took centuries to do:
— transferring loyalty from tribe, caste, sect and village to a single central political community; India had to forge one civic identity across many languages, castes and religions.
— creating an effective centre capable of maintaining law and order, extracting revenue and delivering welfare; India had simultaneously to integrate over five hundred princely states.
Western and World Bank scholars argue these societies will prosper only by modernising and integrating with the world economy, and offer two diagnoses:
describes them as caught between the traditional and the modern, marked by
— a wide gap between the law as written and the law as practised — along with poly-communalism, overlapping functions and the ‘bazaar-canteen’ and ‘sala’ models.
, calls India a state that legislates ambitiously but cannot enforce, so that land-ceiling laws were passed everywhere and implemented almost nowhere, defeating even Nehru.
A.G. Frank, Samir Amin, Immanuel Wallerstein
) locates the cause of backwardness outside these societies altogether, in two propositions:

— the capitalist ‘world system’ is divided into a rich core and a dependent periphery locked into unequal exchange, whereby the periphery exports cheap primary goods and imports costly manufactures — a relation Frank called the ‘development of underdevelopment’.
— the state in the periphery serves this external interest, and the prescribed escape is withdrawal from the world market.

— because the modern state was grafted by colonial rulers onto a traditional agrarian base, its bureaucracy and military were built to subordinate a whole society and now tower over weak indigenous classes — Pakistan becoming a ‘military-bureaucratic oligarchy’ and India acquiring its ‘inspector raj’.
— such a state mediates between the metropolitan bourgeoisie, the native bourgeoisie and the landed classes rather than serving any one of them.

Read together, the two perspectives show the post-colonial state as doubly constrained — by an imported modern form that sits uneasily on a traditional society, and by an inherited economic dependence it did not choose. That is why nation-building and state-building, rather than the classic Western question of how to limit the state, remain its central and unfinished projects.
Q — Critically examine the feminist critique of the state. (UPSC 2021)
Show why feminists deny the state is neutral → lay out the rival feminist streams → assess the remedies they propose.
— the state is not neutral but patriarchal;
: “when I look at the state, it appears male to me.”
— the public/private divide conceals subordination inside the family, on two counts:
— long treated as ‘private’ and left outside the criminal law.
— the state is a potential ally from which women were wrongly excluded; the cure is inclusion.
(One-third of panchayat seats reserved for women by the 73rd Amendment.)
— the welfare state’s benevolence is the cheap way of
(Benefits presume a male breadwinner and fix the woman as carer.)
: men’s political right preceded the social contract.
: patriarchy is a system of power in every relation between the sexes.
: no neutral state without dismantling it.
— the male state rests on military power; two answers to its false neutrality:
: recognise group difference instead of a uniform citizen.
— cooperation and care in place of military strength.
Feminists reject the central liberal assumption that the state is a
Towards a Feminist Theory of the State

, writes that “when I look at the state, it appears male to me”: its law adopts the male point of view as the objective standpoint, so that what counts as consent, provocation or reasonableness is defined from men’s experience. Neutrality of form thus conceals partiality of substance.

The critique rests on this slogan. Liberalism confines politics to the public sphere and treats the household as a private realm beyond regulation; feminists reply that the family is precisely where power, labour and violence are most unequally distributed. The divide is therefore not innocent — it is the mechanism by which women’s subordination is placed beyond political challenge, as two exclusions show:
— it is excluded from national income accounting, so the labour that sustains every household counts for nothing.
— coercion inside the home was long left outside the criminal law as a ‘private’ matter.

) regard the state as a potentially neutral ally from which women were historically and wrongly excluded, and whose remedy is therefore inclusion: the vote, equal legal personality, equal opportunity and representation. India’s reservation of one-third of panchayat seats for women under the 73rd Amendment exemplifies this strategy of using state power to correct exclusion rather than abandoning the state as irredeemable.
are sceptical of that faith. They argue that the welfare state’s apparently benign provision is the cheapest available means of

— someone must feed, nurse and raise the next generation of workers, and unpaid female domestic labour does so at no cost to capital. Welfare policy consequently reinforces the woman’s domestic role and her dependence on a male breadwinner, while extending state surveillance over reproduction and child-rearing.
The critique deepens in three further strikes:

argues that the celebrated social contract was preceded by a sexual contract establishing men’s political right over women, so the masculinist bias lies at the very foundation of modern political theory.
shows patriarchy operating as a system of power in every relationship between the sexes.
draws the conclusion that “without destroying the patriarchal family we cannot get the neutral state.”
Because women are excluded from its making, the state builds its strength on

, generating inter-state tension rather than cooperation and neglecting nature and care. The streams differ on whether to enter, reform or bypass the state, but their common and lasting insight is that genuine neutrality is impossible while patriarchy structures both family and public life; two remedies answer that false neutrality:
would recognise group difference instead of assuming a uniform citizen.
— others argue for a more humane conduct of external relations in place of militarised strength.
Q — Compare the conceptions of the state in Fascism and Marxism, and discuss the Gandhian view and the ‘crisis of legitimacy’ in capitalist societies. (UPSC 2014/2015/2018)
Set Fascism against Marxism → draw the contrast sharply → add Gandhi’s moral rejection → close with the legitimacy crisis of the capitalist state.
: “nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it.”
(The individual exists for the state, never the reverse.)
, the ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’, destined to
— opposites on three counts, twins on one:
— state-worship and permanent dictatorship versus an eventual stateless society.
— nation and race versus class and internationalism.
— private property under state direction versus its abolition.
— both reject liberal democracy and individual autonomy.
— a moral rejection in three steps:
— the state rests on coercion and violates
— Ramrajya of ‘oceanic circles’, self-governing village republics.
— for him the state is the Dalit’s shield, not his enemy.
— welfare demands outrun what capital accumulation can fund; three diagnoses:
: the state can be legitimate or profitable, but struggles to be both.
(Subsidies and loan waivers promised faster than revenue can be raised.)
— from worshipped absolute to doomed class tool to coercive machine — and even the liberal state struggles to reconcile democracy with capitalism.
in itself, in which the individual finds meaning only as a part.
declared: “nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it.” Drawing on
— for whom the state is ‘the march of God on earth’ — it builds a corporate, single-party dictatorship with a cult of the leader, autarky at home and expansion abroad.
dismissed it as an ‘unsystematic doctrine’, while Marxists read it as capitalism in decay defending itself by force.
Marxism, by contrast, treats the state as a

— the ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’ — which exists only because society is divided into classes. It has neither moral value nor permanence: once the dictatorship of the proletariat abolishes private property, the state loses its reason for being and
, the administration of things replacing government over persons.
on three counts and twins on a fourth:
— Fascism culminates in state-worship and permanent dictatorship, Marxism in an eventual stateless society.
— Fascism exalts nation and race, Marxism class and internationalism.
— Fascism retains private property under state direction, Marxism abolishes it.
— yet they converge in method: both reject liberal democracy, parliamentary competition and individual autonomy, and both justify a monopoly party as the vehicle of a higher historical purpose.
Gandhi’s is a moral rejection in three steps:
the state rests on coercion — police, courts and prisons — which stunts self-reliance and violates
, since it represents ‘violence in a concentrated and organised form’.
, a moral order of self-governing village republics arranged in ‘oceanic circles’ rather than a pyramid.
rejected this, insisting that for the Dalit the village is a den of oppression and the state the only instrument of emancipation.
Capitalist democracies face structural ‘crisis tendencies’, diagnosed in three ways:

, argues that democratic politics continually generates demands for welfare and equality whose satisfaction requires taxation and spending that constrain private capital accumulation, so the state can be legitimate or profitable but struggles to be both.
diagnoses this in India, where subsidies and loan waivers are promised faster than revenue can be raised.

Across these conceptions the state ranges from a worshipped absolute in Fascism, to a doomed class tool in Marxism, to a coercive machine to be morally transcended in Gandhi. The legitimacy-crisis debate completes the picture by showing that even the liberal-capitalist state, which claims to have escaped all three critiques, struggles to reconcile the promises of democracy with the requirements of capitalism.
: the state has the ‘monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory’.
absolute, universal, permanent, indivisible, inalienable; ‘law = command of the sovereign’ (Austin).
: ‘since society is federal, authority should also be federal’;
: ‘sovereignty must be expunged from political theory’.
Thatcher, Reagan, WTO, Washington Consensus (‘trade not aid’); India’s 1991 LPG reforms.
economic base determines the political superstructure (the state); state ‘withers away’ in communism.
= hegemony (rule by consent, not force alone).
: the pluralist state has ‘no single source of authority… divisible in parts’;
: groups are unequal (‘survival of the fittest’).
: globalization vs sovereignty is ‘not a zero-sum game’ (transformationalist).
neutral/minimal ‘necessary evil’; negative → positive → neo-liberal; neo-liberalism = globalization’s ideology; critique = inequality + legitimacy crisis.
class instrument; materialist base→superstructure; instrumentalist (Marx/Lenin/Miliband) vs structuralist relative autonomy (Poulantzas); Gramscian hegemony; withers away.
attacks monistic/Austinian sovereignty; power dispersed among associations (Laski/MacIver); moderate vs extreme; realistic but ‘inconsistent’.
Hobbes’ first full theory; porous ‘hard shell’; globalists vs state-centric vs transformationalist (Held); crisis of nation-state.
nation- + state-building; modernization (Riggs, Myrdal) vs Marxist dependency (Frank/Wallerstein) & Alavi’s overdeveloped state.
state is patriarchal (MacKinnon); ‘personal is political’; liberal vs Marxist-feminist vs radical (Pateman/Okin); differentiated citizenship (Young).
Fascism = state worship (Mussolini) vs Marxism = withering; Gandhi = soulless machine → enlightened anarchy; Habermas = legitimation crisis.

Mussolini — ‘nothing beyond the State’; Marx — ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’; MacKinnon — ‘the state appears male’; Hayek — ‘social justice is a mirage’; Laski — ‘society is federal, so authority must be federal’.

contentText: Syllabus — Theories of the State: Liberal, Neo-liberal, Marxist, Pluralist, Post-colonial and Feminist. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 2) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the concept & elements of the state; theories of sovereignty (monistic/Austin vs pluralist) and the impact of globalization on sovereignty; and the six theories of the state — Liberal (negative, positive, neo-liberal), Marxist (instrumentalist & structuralist), Pluralist, Post-colonial and Feminist — plus the Fascist, Gandhian and legitimacy-crisis conceptions and the crisis of the modern nation-state. Must-know thinkers:  Hobbes, Locke, Austin, Laski, MacIver, Krabbe, Marx, Engels, Lenin, Miliband, Poulantzas, Gramsci, Robert Dahl, C. Wright Mills, Kenichi Ohmae, David Held, Edward Said, Hamza Alavi, A.G. Frank, Wallerstein, Gunnar Myrdal, F.W. Riggs, Catherine MacKinnon, Carole Pateman, Mussolini, Gandhi, Habermas. PYQ trend:  the heaviest-scoring unit. Neo-liberal state (2016/17/18), Feminist (2021), Post-colonial (2020), Pluralist (2019), Marxist & materialism (2013/14), sovereignty & globalization (2015), Gandhi (2015), Fascism (2014/18), legitimacy crisis (2015), Hobbesian obligation (2017). Master Questions Q — Trace the evolution of the liberal theory of the state through its negative, positive and neo-liberal phases, and critically examine the neo-liberal conception of the state and its link with globalization. (UPSC 2016/2017/2018) What it’s asking:  Tell the story of liberalism in three phases → then judge neo-liberalism and its marriage with globalization. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core idea  — a neutral, limited state resting on consent;  Paine’s  ‘necessary evil’.  (The state is the referee, not a player — it enforces the rules of the market but never picks the winner.) 2. Negative phase  —  Smith, Bentham, Spencer  build it on two pillars:    2.1 Laissez-faire  — the state keeps law and order and enforces contracts — nothing more.    2.2 Negative liberty  — the simple absence of interference, so the less the state does the freer the citizen. 3. Positive phase  —  J.S. Mill, Green, Hobhouse  recast it in two moves:    3.1 Agency of common good  — the state creates the conditions of self-development.    3.2 Positive liberty  — free speech is empty for a hungry illiterate — hence MGNREGA and the Right to Education. 4. Neo-liberal phase  —  Hayek, Friedman, Nozick  roll the welfare ‘nanny state’ back on three counts:    4.1 Night-watchman state  — India’s 1991 LPG reforms: the licence raj dismantled, PSUs disinvested.    4.2 Primacy of economic liberty  —  Friedman : economic freedom is a precondition of political freedom.    4.3 No redistribution  —  Hayek : ‘social justice is a mirage’. 5. Globalization link  — neo-liberalism became globalization’s ideology through three carriers:    5.1 Thatcher and Reagan  — the doctrine adopted by the leading states and exported as ‘shock therapy’.    5.2 Washington Consensus  — deregulation, privatisation and ‘trade not aid’.    5.3 The WTO  — IMF loans carried structural-adjustment conditions, as with India in 1991. 6. Critique & conclusion  — widening inequality breeds a  legitimacy crisis ;  Sen  and  Stiglitz  push back.  (The 2008 bailouts brought the state straight back.) Model Answer 1. Core idea.  The liberal theory sees the state as a  neutral, limited instrument  that exists to protect individual rights and freedom and rests on the  consent of the people . It is a referee rather than a player: it lays down and enforces the rules within which individuals pursue their own ends, but does not prescribe those ends.  Thomas Paine  caught the ambivalence in calling it a ‘necessary evil’ — evil because every law restricts freedom, necessary because freedom cannot be safeguarded without it. From this single premise the doctrine evolved through three phases. 2. Negative phase.  Classical or negative liberalism ( Adam Smith, Bentham, James Mill, Herbert Spencer ) begins from the rational individual possessing inalienable rights to life, liberty and property. From that premise it builds two pillars:    2.1 Laissez-faire  — the state must confine itself to defence, law and order and the enforcement of contracts, since the market coordinates society better than any minister can.    2.2 Negative liberty  — liberty is the mere absence of external interference, so that the less the state does, the freer the citizen is held to be. 3. Positive phase.  By the late nineteenth century laissez-faire had produced liberty without equality, and welfare liberals ( J.S. Mill, T.H. Green, Hobhouse ) recast the state in two connected moves:    3.1 Agency of the common good  — the state becomes responsible for the conditions of self-development, which require education, health and a floor of income.    3.2 Positive liberty  — liberty is not being left alone but possessing the actual capacity for self-development. Freedom of speech means little to a hungry illiterate; hence the welfare state, and in India measures such as MGNREGA and the Right to Education, are read as enabling rather than restricting freedom. 4. Neo-liberal phase.  Neo-liberalism or libertarianism ( Hayek, Friedman, Nozick ) is a reaction against this interventionist ‘nanny state’, which it charges with inefficiency, dependence and creeping serfdom. Its programme has three elements:    4.1 The night-watchman state  — the state is rolled back to its minimal functions; India’s 1991 liberalisation, dismantling the licence raj and disinvesting public undertakings, is the clearest domestic instance.    4.2 Primacy of economic liberty  — “economic freedom is a precondition of political freedom” ( Friedman ).    4.3 Rejection of redistribution  —  Hayek  declares that “social justice is a mirage” because market outcomes are unintended and so cannot be called unjust. 5. Globalization link.  Neo-liberalism became the ruling ideology of globalization, carried by three vehicles:    5.1 Thatcher and Reagan  — adopted by  Thatcher  and  Reagan , it was exported through ‘shock therapy’ and structural adjustment.    5.2 The Washington Consensus  — deregulation, privatisation and ‘trade not aid’.    5.3 The WTO and conditionalities  — the  WTO  was its institutional high point, and loans carried conditionalities obliging borrowing states to shrink themselves, as India experienced in 1991; hence the examiner’s proposition that “the political ideology of globalization is neo-liberalism.” 6. Critique and conclusion.  By overestimating the individual and underestimating the state, liberalism builds a capitalist order that can serve exploitative ends, and neo-liberalism’s widening inequality has produced a  legitimacy crisis  for it.  Amartya Sen , for whom development is the expansion of capabilities, and  Joseph Stiglitz , who exposes the asymmetries of globalization, therefore argue for a balanced, welfare-oriented state — a case vindicated by the post-2008 return of massive state intervention. Q — Examine the Marxist theory of the state — its origin, its instrumentalist and relative-autonomy (structuralist) variants, and its materialist basis. (UPSC 2013/2014) What it’s asking:  Show why the state is a class weapon → prove the materialist basis → contrast the two Marxist variants → end with withering away. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core claim  — the state is not neutral but a  class institution  born of force, not contract ( Engels ).  (The colonial state’s law protected the planter, never the tenant.) 2. Materialist basis  — politics rests on economics, in two tiers:    2.1 Base  — the mode of production and whoever owns the means of production.    2.2 Superstructure  — law, politics and ideas, the state among them.  (Whoever owns the factory shapes who writes the factory law.) 3. Instrumentalist variant  —  Marx, Lenin, Miliband : the state is the ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’.  (Even the welfare state left wealth concentrated and the bureaucracy elitist.) 4. Structuralist variant  —  Poulantzas, Althusser : the state has  relative autonomy , in two senses:    4.1 Equilibrium-maker  — it may act against individual capitalists to save capitalism itself, legislating a minimum wage in calm times.    4.2 Autonomy only relative  — but it bails out the banks in a crash — 2008. 5. Hegemony & withering away  — two further propositions:    5.1 Hegemony  —  Gramsci : rule works by consent, not coercion alone.  (Schools and the press make the ruler’s worldview feel like common sense.)    5.2 Withering away  — the state lasts only as long as classes do. 6. Critique & conclusion  —  Dahl : not all conflict is class conflict; yet no theory exposes the state’s hidden class bias better. Model Answer 1. Core claim.  Marxism is above all a critique of the liberal-capitalist state. Against the liberal claim of neutrality it argues that the state is a  class institution  — an instrument of organised coercion serving whichever class owns the means of production. Its origin lies not in a social contract but in  force  and in the splitting of society into contending classes: for  Engels , in  The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State , the state arises precisely when class antagonism becomes unmanageable — as the colonial state’s codes protected the planter and never the tenant. 2. Materialist basis.  Marx’s understanding is materialistic because politics is determined by economics, society being read in two tiers:    2.1 The base  — the mode of production and the class owning it; whoever owns the factory ultimately shapes who writes the factory law.    2.2 The superstructure  — law, politics, religion and ideas, the state among them, all determined by the base. Political power is thus ‘the organised power of one class for oppressing another’, and ‘the ruling ideas of every age are the ideas of the ruling class’: the state cannot float free of the property relations that sustain it. 3. Instrumentalist variant.  On the instrumentalist reading ( Marx, Lenin, Ralph Miliband ) the state is a direct tool in the hands of the capitalists — “the executive committee of the bourgeoisie” ( Marx ), which “represents the irreconcilability of class antagonism” ( Lenin ).  Miliband , in  The State in Capitalist Society , showed empirically that even in the post-war welfare state wealth remained concentrated and the higher bureaucracy, judiciary and army were recruited from the propertied elite — exploding the myth of a ‘managerial revolution’. 4. Structuralist variant.  The structuralists ( Poulantzas, Althusser ), building on Marx’s  The 18th Brumaire , hold that the state enjoys  relative autonomy , which works in two directions:    4.1 Equilibrium-maker above classes  — it is not a puppet, and where no single class is dominant it can act as an ‘equilibrium-maker’ above classes, as under Bonapartism, thereby appearing neutral. It may even legislate against particular capitalists — a minimum wage, a factory safety law — in order to preserve capitalism as a whole.    4.2 Autonomy only relative  — in a genuine crisis it intervenes for the rich, as the 2008 bank bailouts amid ‘Occupy Wall Street’ revealed. 5. Hegemony and withering away.  Two further propositions complete the theory:    5.1 Hegemony  —  Antonio Gramsci  showed that class rule survives less through force than through the manufacture of consent in civil society, so that schools, churches and newspapers make the ruling class’s worldview feel like plain common sense.    5.2 Withering away  — the state is nevertheless historical, not eternal: it exists only as long as classes exist, and once the dictatorship of the proletariat has abolished private property it will ‘wither away’ in a classless communist society. 6. Critique and conclusion.  Robert Dahl  and the pluralists object that the theory reduces all conflict to class conflict, ignoring the real competition of religious, linguistic, regional and professional groups, while twentieth-century experience suggests the state does not wither but hardens. Yet the Marxist theory remains the sharpest available exposure of the class bias concealed behind the state’s claim to neutrality. Q — Critically examine the pluralist theory of the state and sovereignty as an attack on the monistic (Austinian) theory. (UPSC 2019) What it’s asking:  State the monistic doctrine → mount the pluralist attack → grade the pluralists → weigh the charge of inconsistency. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The monistic theory  —  Hobbes, Austin : one  absolute, indivisible, inalienable  sovereign; ‘law is the command of the sovereign’.  (Sovereignty = the last word that no one may lawfully answer back.) 2. The pluralist attack  —  Laski, MacIver : the state is only  one association among many .  (A citizen’s life is ruled as much by her union, caste panchayat, temple and university.) 3. Laski’s formula  — “since society is federal, authority should also be federal”;  Krabbe : sovereignty must be ‘expunged from political theory’.  (India’s Seventh Schedule and the 73rd Amendment are federal authority in practice.) 4. Two grades of pluralism  — pluralists differ in degree:    4.1 Moderate  —  Laski : the state is still ‘the keystone of the social architecture’.    4.2 Extreme  —  MacIver : the ‘service state’ “commands because it serves”. 5. Critique  — three charges:    5.1 Inconsistency  — it attacks the state yet keeps it — ‘cake and eat it too’.    5.2 Unequal groups  —  C. Wright Mills : a ‘power elite’ dominates the rest.    5.3 No state ever fitted the model  —  Henry Maine : not even Ranjit Singh’s Punjab matched Austin. 6. Conclusion  — inconsistency is not irrelevance: dispersed power fits an age of federalism, the UN and the EU better than war-prone monism. Model Answer 1. The monistic theory.  The  monistic or Austinian theory  holds that in every independent political society there must exist one determinate sovereign whose power is  absolute, universal, permanent, indivisible and inalienable .  John Austin  put it formally: if a determinate human superior, not habitually obeying any other superior, receives habitual obedience from the bulk of a given society, that superior is sovereign and ‘law is the command of the sovereign’. Sovereignty is thus the last word to which no one may lawfully answer back — a position echoed in  Weber’s  definition of the state by its monopoly of legitimate force, and rooted in  Hobbes’s  undivided Leviathan. 2. The pluralist attack.  Pluralists ( Laski, MacIver, Figgis, Barker ) deny that any single centre can absorb all authority. Human beings pursue many interests through many associations, so power should be  distributed  among them; the state is  one association among many , not their master, and cannot satisfy the whole of human need. A citizen’s conduct in India is in fact governed as much by her trade union, caste panchayat, religious body and university as by Parliament, and each of these commands a genuine loyalty of its own. 3. Laski’s formula.  Harold Laski  compressed the argument into a maxim: “since society is federal, authority should also be federal.” Sovereignty must be functionally divided among the groups that actually perform society’s work, and obedience must be earned rather than commanded.  Krabbe  went further, insisting that “the notion of sovereignty must be expunged from political theory” and replaced by the sovereignty of law and the community’s sense of right. The Indian Constitution’s distribution of powers in the Seventh Schedule and the devolution effected by the 73rd Amendment illustrate such federal authority in practice. 4. Two grades of pluralism.  Pluralists differ in degree:    4.1 Moderate pluralists  —  Laski  still makes the state ‘the keystone of the social architecture’, because it alone can resolve conflicts between associations and command the widest allegiance.    4.2 Extreme pluralists  —  MacIver  allows it no primacy at all: the ‘service state’ “commands because it serves” and is ‘both the guardian and the child of law’, so its authority is derivative and conditional. 5. Critique.  Three charges are pressed against the theory:    5.1 Inconsistency  — it attacks the state’s supremacy yet, unlike anarchism, retains the state, so critics say ‘pluralists want to keep the cake and eat it too’.    5.2 Unequal associations  — it assumes associations compete on equal terms, whereas  C. Wright Mills  shows a ‘power elite’ of corporate, military and political leaders dominating the rest, a survival of the fittest among groups.    5.3 The historical objection  —  Henry Maine  adds that no historical state, Ranjit Singh’s Punjab included, ever matched Austin’s model either. 6. Conclusion.  Inconsistency, however, is not irrelevance. By dispersing power, dignifying associations and taking international law seriously, pluralism describes an age of federalism, the United Nations, the ICJ and the European Union far better than the monistic doctrine, and by denying any state an absolute will it is also the more conducive to peace. Q — Discuss the theories of sovereignty and examine the challenges posed by globalization to the sovereignty of the modern nation-state. (UPSC 2015) What it’s asking:  Define sovereignty and its rival theories → then test how far globalization and internal strains have hollowed it out. Gist — the spine to recall 1. What sovereignty is  — the supreme, final law-making power;  Hobbes  gave its first full theory.  (Only Parliament can bind every person within India’s territory.) 2. Rival theories  — two rival accounts:    2.1 Monistic  —  Austin : absolute and indivisible.    2.2 Pluralist  —  Laski, MacIver : shared with associations. 3. Globalization’s challenge  — the state’s ‘hard shell’ turns  porous  ( Ohmae’s   Borderless World ) on four fronts:    3.1 Information technology  — data and ideas cross frontiers freely.    3.2 Market integration  — capital exits at a keystroke.    3.3 International organisations and law  — a WTO ruling can unsettle a national farm subsidy.    3.4 Global civil society  — NGOs and movements press from below. 4. Three perspectives  — no consensus on how far this goes:    4.1 Globalists  — sovereignty really is diluted.    4.2 State-centric  — states are still in control.    4.3 Transformationalist  —  Held : ‘not a zero-sum game’. 5. Internal challenges  — the strain also comes from within:    5.1 Stateless nations  — the Kurds deny the congruence of nation and state.    5.2 Multi-ethnic break-ups  — the collapse of the USSR and Yugoslavia.    5.3 Nuclear insecurity  — no state can any longer guarantee security. 6. Conclusion  — sovereignty is not extinguished but  reconfigured .  (The EU pools it; climate and trade treaties make India accept limits it writes itself.) Model Answer 1. What sovereignty is.  Sovereignty — the supreme and final power to make and enforce law within a territory — is the defining attribute of the modern nation-state and, with population, territory and government, one of its four elements.  Hobbes  supplied its first complete theory in  Leviathan , where subjects surrender their right of self-government to a single undivided sovereign in exchange for security. In practical terms it means that only Parliament may bind every person within India’s territory, and that externally no other state may command it. 2. Rival theories.  Classically sovereignty is  absolute, universal, permanent, indivisible and inalienable , but two rival accounts divide the field:    2.1 The monistic view  — that of  Austin , for whom law is simply the command of the sovereign backed by sanction.    2.2 The pluralist view  —  Laski  and  MacIver  insist that authority is shared with the many associations of a federal society, while  Krabbe  would abolish the concept altogether. The globalization debate is in effect the empirical continuation of this old theoretical quarrel. 3. Globalization’s challenge.  If the nation-state is a ‘billiard ball with a hard shell’, globalization has made that shell  porous  —  Kenichi Ohmae , in  The Borderless World , concludes that political boundaries are fading as ‘global citizens’ and transnational firms escape state control. The shell is breached on four fronts:    3.1 Information technology  — it carries data and ideas past frontiers.    3.2 Market integration  — it lets capital exit at a keystroke, disciplining national economic policy.    3.3 International organisations and law  — they bind states from above, so that a WTO ruling can unsettle a national farm subsidy.    3.4 Global civil society  — NGOs and movements press from below. 4. Three perspectives.  There is no consensus on how far this goes:    4.1 Globalists  —  Ohmae, McLuhan  hold that sovereignty is genuinely diluted both internally and externally.    4.2 The state-centric school  —  Gilpin, Kapstein  reply that the world remains state-centric and that globalization is itself a policy states chose and can reverse.    4.3 Transformationalists  —  David Held  mediates: globalization is ‘not a zero-sum game’ — in some domains the state loses, in others it gains new regulatory reach — while  Sorensen  notes that weak and strong states are affected very unequally. 5. Internal challenges.  The nation-state is strained from within as well, on three counts:    5.1 Stateless nations  — peoples such as the  Kurds  deny the congruence of nation and state.    5.2 Multi-ethnic break-up  — federations have disintegrated, as in the USSR and Yugoslavia, while sub-nationalism and diaspora loyalties divide allegiance.    5.3 Nuclear insecurity  — nuclear weapons mean no state can any longer guarantee the security that was sovereignty’s original justification — producing a ‘global village’ of shared risks, from pandemics to climate change. 6. Conclusion.  Sovereignty is therefore not extinguished but  reconfigured : because global problems demand collective solutions, states now accept self-imposed adjustments to their own authority, as the European Union’s pooling of sovereignty and India’s climate and trade commitments show.  Susan Strange  rightly urges that economics and politics be studied together to grasp this shift of authority from states to markets. Q — Analyse the post-colonial theory of the state through the modernization and Marxist (dependency/structuralist) perspectives. (UPSC 2020) What it’s asking:  Say what makes the post-colonial state distinctive → then read it twice over, once through modernization and once through Marxism. Gist — the spine to recall 1. What it studies  — newly independent ‘third world’ states still shaped by colonialism;  Nkrumah’s   neo-colonialism .  (Flag independence, while the economy still ships raw material to the old metropolis.) 2. The twin task  — two jobs the West never faced at once:    2.1 Nation-building  — forging one shared identity across language, caste and religion.    2.2 State-building  — creating effective authority; India integrated 500-odd princely states. 3. Modernization view  — two diagnoses of the gap between law and practice:    3.1 Prismatic society  —  Riggs : formalism, the law on paper differs from the law in the village.    3.2 Soft state  —  Myrdal : land-ceiling laws passed everywhere, enforced almost nowhere. 4. Marxist dependency  —  Frank, Amin, Wallerstein  locate the cause outside:    4.1 Core and periphery  — a rich core and a dependent periphery in unequal exchange — the ‘development of underdevelopment’.    4.2 De-linking  — escape lies in withdrawing from the world market. 5. Structuralist view  —  Alavi’s   overdeveloped state , on two counts:    5.1 Imported apparatus  — a bureaucracy and army towering over a traditional base.  (Pakistan as a military-bureaucratic oligarchy; India’s ‘inspector raj’.)    5.2 Relative autonomy  — it mediates between metropolitan bourgeoisie, native bourgeoisie and landed classes rather than serving one. 6. Conclusion  — caught between an imported form and inherited economic dependence, its nation- and state-building remain unfinished. Model Answer 1. What it studies.  Post-colonial theory is not a fresh general theory of the state but an attempt to analyse the  newly independent ‘third world’ states  whose politics remains shaped by their colonial past. Formal independence coexists with continuing economic and cultural domination — a  neo-colonialism , the term coined by  Kwame Nkrumah , in which a country flies its own flag while still exporting raw material to its former metropolis.  Edward Said  (in  Orientalism ) and  Gayatri Spivak  stress how deeply this legacy penetrates knowledge and identity themselves. 2. The twin task.  Such states confront a  twin task  the Western state never faced simultaneously, attempting in decades what Europe took centuries to do:    2.1 Nation-building  — transferring loyalty from tribe, caste, sect and village to a single central political community; India had to forge one civic identity across many languages, castes and religions.    2.2 State-building  — creating an effective centre capable of maintaining law and order, extracting revenue and delivering welfare; India had simultaneously to integrate over five hundred princely states. 3. Modernization view.  Western and World Bank scholars argue these societies will prosper only by modernising and integrating with the world economy, and offer two diagnoses:    3.1 The prismatic society  —  F.W. Riggs  describes them as caught between the traditional and the modern, marked by  formalism  — a wide gap between the law as written and the law as practised — along with poly-communalism, overlapping functions and the ‘bazaar-canteen’ and ‘sala’ models.    3.2 The soft state  —  Gunnar Myrdal , in  Asian Drama , calls India a state that legislates ambitiously but cannot enforce, so that land-ceiling laws were passed everywhere and implemented almost nowhere, defeating even Nehru. 4. Marxist dependency perspective.  The  dependency  or instrumentalist approach ( A.G. Frank, Samir Amin, Immanuel Wallerstein ) locates the cause of backwardness outside these societies altogether, in two propositions:    4.1 Core and periphery  — the capitalist ‘world system’ is divided into a rich core and a dependent periphery locked into unequal exchange, whereby the periphery exports cheap primary goods and imports costly manufactures — a relation Frank called the ‘development of underdevelopment’.    4.2 De-linking  — the state in the periphery serves this external interest, and the prescribed escape is withdrawal from the world market. 5. Structuralist view.  The  structuralist  approach of  Hamza Alavi  calls the post-colonial state  ‘overdeveloped’ , on two counts:    5.1 An imported apparatus  — because the modern state was grafted by colonial rulers onto a traditional agrarian base, its bureaucracy and military were built to subordinate a whole society and now tower over weak indigenous classes — Pakistan becoming a ‘military-bureaucratic oligarchy’ and India acquiring its ‘inspector raj’.    5.2 Relative autonomy  — such a state mediates between the metropolitan bourgeoisie, the native bourgeoisie and the landed classes rather than serving any one of them. 6. Conclusion.  Read together, the two perspectives show the post-colonial state as doubly constrained — by an imported modern form that sits uneasily on a traditional society, and by an inherited economic dependence it did not choose. That is why nation-building and state-building, rather than the classic Western question of how to limit the state, remain its central and unfinished projects. Q — Critically examine the feminist critique of the state. (UPSC 2021) What it’s asking:  Show why feminists deny the state is neutral → lay out the rival feminist streams → assess the remedies they propose. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core claim  — the state is not neutral but patriarchal;  MacKinnon : “when I look at the state, it appears male to me.” 2. ‘The personal is political’  — the public/private divide conceals subordination inside the family, on two counts:    2.1 Unpaid domestic work  — excluded from national income accounting.    2.2 Violence within marriage  — long treated as ‘private’ and left outside the criminal law. 3. Liberal feminists  — the state is a potential ally from which women were wrongly excluded; the cure is inclusion.  (One-third of panchayat seats reserved for women by the 73rd Amendment.) 4. Marxist-feminists  — the welfare state’s benevolence is the cheap way of  reproducing labour power .  (Benefits presume a male breadwinner and fix the woman as carer.) 5. Radical critique  — three deeper strikes:    5.1 The sexual contract  —  Pateman’s   The Sexual Contract : men’s political right preceded the social contract.    5.2 Sexual politics  —  Millett : patriarchy is a system of power in every relation between the sexes.    5.3 The patriarchal family  —  Okin : no neutral state without dismantling it. 6. Remedies & conclusion  — the male state rests on military power; two answers to its false neutrality:    6.1 Differentiated citizenship  —  Young : recognise group difference instead of a uniform citizen.    6.2 Feminist foreign policy  — cooperation and care in place of military strength. Model Answer 1. Core claim.  Feminists reject the central liberal assumption that the state is a  neutral  arbiter standing above social divisions.  Catherine MacKinnon , in  Towards a Feminist Theory of the State , writes that “when I look at the state, it appears male to me”: its law adopts the male point of view as the objective standpoint, so that what counts as consent, provocation or reasonableness is defined from men’s experience. Neutrality of form thus conceals partiality of substance. 2. ‘The personal is political’.  The critique rests on this slogan. Liberalism confines politics to the public sphere and treats the household as a private realm beyond regulation; feminists reply that the family is precisely where power, labour and violence are most unequally distributed. The divide is therefore not innocent — it is the mechanism by which women’s subordination is placed beyond political challenge, as two exclusions show:    2.1 Unpaid domestic work  — it is excluded from national income accounting, so the labour that sustains every household counts for nothing.    2.2 Violence within marriage  — coercion inside the home was long left outside the criminal law as a ‘private’ matter. 3. Liberal feminists.  Liberal feminists  ( Wollstonecraft, Betty Friedan ) regard the state as a potentially neutral ally from which women were historically and wrongly excluded, and whose remedy is therefore inclusion: the vote, equal legal personality, equal opportunity and representation. India’s reservation of one-third of panchayat seats for women under the 73rd Amendment exemplifies this strategy of using state power to correct exclusion rather than abandoning the state as irredeemable. 4. Marxist-feminists.  Marxist-feminists  are sceptical of that faith. They argue that the welfare state’s apparently benign provision is the cheapest available means of  reproducing labour power  — someone must feed, nurse and raise the next generation of workers, and unpaid female domestic labour does so at no cost to capital. Welfare policy consequently reinforces the woman’s domestic role and her dependence on a male breadwinner, while extending state surveillance over reproduction and child-rearing. 5. Radical critique.  The critique deepens in three further strikes:    5.1 The sexual contract  —  Carole Pateman’s   The Sexual Contract  argues that the celebrated social contract was preceded by a sexual contract establishing men’s political right over women, so the masculinist bias lies at the very foundation of modern political theory.    5.2 Sexual politics  —  Kate Millett  shows patriarchy operating as a system of power in every relationship between the sexes.    5.3 The patriarchal family  —  Susanne Moller Okin  draws the conclusion that “without destroying the patriarchal family we cannot get the neutral state.” 6. Remedies and conclusion.  Because women are excluded from its making, the state builds its strength on  military power , generating inter-state tension rather than cooperation and neglecting nature and care. The streams differ on whether to enter, reform or bypass the state, but their common and lasting insight is that genuine neutrality is impossible while patriarchy structures both family and public life; two remedies answer that false neutrality:    6.1 Differentiated citizenship  —  Iris Marion Young  would recognise group difference instead of assuming a uniform citizen.    6.2 A feminist foreign policy  — others argue for a more humane conduct of external relations in place of militarised strength. Q — Compare the conceptions of the state in Fascism and Marxism, and discuss the Gandhian view and the ‘crisis of legitimacy’ in capitalist societies. (UPSC 2014/2015/2018) What it’s asking:  Set Fascism against Marxism → draw the contrast sharply → add Gandhi’s moral rejection → close with the legitimacy crisis of the capitalist state. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Fascist state  — an  absolute, totalitarian end  in itself;  Mussolini : “nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it.”  (The individual exists for the state, never the reverse.) 2. Marxist state  — a  temporary class instrument , the ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’, destined to  wither away  once classes end. 3. The contrast  — opposites on three counts, twins on one:    3.1 Destination  — state-worship and permanent dictatorship versus an eventual stateless society.    3.2 Loyalty  — nation and race versus class and internationalism.    3.3 Property  — private property under state direction versus its abolition.    3.4 Common enemy  — both reject liberal democracy and individual autonomy. 4. Gandhi’s view  — a moral rejection in three steps:    4.1 A ‘soulless machine’  — the state rests on coercion and violates  Ahimsa .    4.2 Enlightened anarchy  — Ramrajya of ‘oceanic circles’, self-governing village republics.    4.3 Ambedkar’s dissent  — for him the state is the Dalit’s shield, not his enemy. 5. Crisis of legitimacy  — welfare demands outrun what capital accumulation can fund; three diagnoses:    5.1 Legitimation crisis  —  Habermas : the state can be legitimate or profitable, but struggles to be both.    5.2 Government overload  —  Anthony King .    5.3 Crisis of governability  —  Kohli  on India.  (Subsidies and loan waivers promised faster than revenue can be raised.) 6. Conclusion  — from worshipped absolute to doomed class tool to coercive machine — and even the liberal state struggles to reconcile democracy with capitalism. Model Answer 1. Fascist state.  Fascism  glorifies the state as an  absolute, totalitarian end  in itself, in which the individual finds meaning only as a part.  Mussolini  declared: “nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it.” Drawing on  Hegel  — for whom the state is ‘the march of God on earth’ — it builds a corporate, single-party dictatorship with a cult of the leader, autarky at home and expansion abroad.  Laski  dismissed it as an ‘unsystematic doctrine’, while Marxists read it as capitalism in decay defending itself by force. 2. Marxist state.  Marxism, by contrast, treats the state as a  temporary class instrument  — the ‘executive committee of the bourgeoisie’ — which exists only because society is divided into classes. It has neither moral value nor permanence: once the dictatorship of the proletariat abolishes private property, the state loses its reason for being and  ‘withers away’ , the administration of things replacing government over persons. 3. The contrast.  The two doctrines are  exact opposites  on three counts and twins on a fourth:    3.1 Destination  — Fascism culminates in state-worship and permanent dictatorship, Marxism in an eventual stateless society.    3.2 Loyalty  — Fascism exalts nation and race, Marxism class and internationalism.    3.3 Property  — Fascism retains private property under state direction, Marxism abolishes it.    3.4 Common enemy  — yet they converge in method: both reject liberal democracy, parliamentary competition and individual autonomy, and both justify a monopoly party as the vehicle of a higher historical purpose. 4. Gandhi’s view.  Gandhi’s is a moral rejection in three steps:    4.1 The ‘soulless machine’  — for  Gandhi  the state rests on coercion — police, courts and prisons — which stunts self-reliance and violates  Ahimsa , since it represents ‘violence in a concentrated and organised form’.    4.2 Enlightened anarchy  — drawing on Thoreau and  Tolstoy , he would dissolve it through  Swaraj  understood as self-control, into  Ramrajya , a moral order of self-governing village republics arranged in ‘oceanic circles’ rather than a pyramid.    4.3 Ambedkar’s dissent  —  Ambedkar  rejected this, insisting that for the Dalit the village is a den of oppression and the state the only instrument of emancipation. 5. Crisis of legitimacy.  Capitalist democracies face structural ‘crisis tendencies’, diagnosed in three ways:    5.1 Legitimation crisis  —  Jurgen Habermas , in  Legitimation Crisis , argues that democratic politics continually generates demands for welfare and equality whose satisfaction requires taxation and spending that constrain private capital accumulation, so the state can be legitimate or profitable but struggles to be both.    5.2 Government overload  —  Anthony King  calls the result ‘government overload’.    5.3 Crisis of governability  —  Atul Kohli  diagnoses this in India, where subsidies and loan waivers are promised faster than revenue can be raised. 6. Conclusion.  Across these conceptions the state ranges from a worshipped absolute in Fascism, to a doomed class tool in Marxism, to a coercive machine to be morally transcended in Gandhi. The legitimacy-crisis debate completes the picture by showing that even the liberal-capitalist state, which claims to have escaped all three critiques, struggles to reconcile the promises of democracy with the requirements of capitalism.
